job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Issues in S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6, 2026)

Items are numbered continuously. Some cut against us, and I've noted those. I reviewed only the text you provided, so legal should check whether the introduced version differs and whether any item is already fixed elsewhere.

1. **§2(1)(A):** The 10,000-ton threshold applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could split recovery across several vessels, each under the threshold, and fall outside the definition. "Per year" and "recovery" are also undefined (wet or dry weight, whether sediment counts, calendar or rolling year), so the measurement point is open.

2. **§2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" has no antecedent. Section 2 doesn't say which Secretary, and §6 uses "Secretary of State," so the reference is ambiguous. The clause also sets no criteria, procedure, or notice for finding a "comparable" risk, which invites a vagueness challenge and leaves scope to agency discretion.

3. **§2(1):** "Commercial" and "mining" are never defined beyond the tonnage test. A pilot, test, or stockpiling operation below 10,000 tons per year, or recovery without sale, arguably falls outside the definition.

4. **§2(2):** "U.S. person" covers citizens and State-organized corporations only. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and foreign-incorporated subsidiaries, which narrows the "anywhere" reach in §3(a). Legal should confirm how our corporate structure fits this definition.

5. **§2(3) and §3(a):** The prohibition in §3 applies to any commercial mining regardless of vessel, but "covered vessel" (over 5,000 gross tons, "equipped for" recovery, undefined) controls only the registry in §4. A smaller vessel could be prohibited but never registered, which is an enforcement gap.

6. **§3(a):** "In the United States" is undefined for the territorial sea, EEZ, continental shelf, high seas, and the Area. Non-U.S. persons and foreign-flagged vessels operating in international waters may be outside the Act's reach. This is the central jurisdictional gap.

7. **§3(a):** "Engage in" is undefined. The prohibition doesn't clearly reach financing, equipment supply, chartering, or processing, so activities could be split among affiliated entities to avoid it.

8. **§3(a):** There is no import or sale prohibition. Metals or nodule products recovered abroad could still be imported and sold in the U.S., which limits the Act's practical effect on supply.

9. **§3(b):** "Exploration license" is undefined and doesn't name the issuing authority. It's unclear whether DSHMRA exploration licenses, Area contracts sponsored through foreign states, or other instruments qualify. If our international operations rely on contracts that aren't U.S. "licenses," they may not be grandfathered.

10. **§3(b):** The exemption protects "mining conducted under" an exploration license, not exploration itself. Read literally, it covers commercial-scale recovery with no volume, area, or time cap. This may be the largest loophole in the bill. Separately, it doesn't mention DSHMRA commercial recovery permits, so a pending permit application may not be protected.

11. **§3(b):** The clause doesn't address renewals, extensions, amendments, expanded areas, license transfers, or replacement licenses for the same area after enactment.

12. **§3(c):** "Environmental assessment" is undefined. The exemption has no volume cap, duration limit, approval requirement, or reporting, and "for the purpose of" is subjective. Commercial recovery could be recharacterized as assessment.

13. **§4(a):** "Operator" is undefined, so owner, charterer, and operator obligations are unclear. The registration requirement sets no deadline or content and doesn't tie to any permission, so it operates as a notice rather than an authorization.

14. **§4(b):** Reports must describe "recovery activities" but specify no content (tonnage, location, dates), no deadline within the quarter, and no confidentiality or disclosure rule. The certification has no penalty for false statements beyond general law.

15. **§4 and §5(a):** Civil penalties attach only to violations of §3. Failure to register or report under §4 carries no penalty in the Act, so the registry is effectively unenforceable. (Critics will likely want this fixed, so expect it to be corrected at markup.)

16. **§5(a):** No agency is named to enforce civil penalties, and the Act sets no procedure for notice, hearing, assessment, or civil action (for example, who sues in court).

17. **§5(a):** "Each day on which the violation occurs" has no definition for continuing violations or for counting a single voyage. The clause also sets no minimum and no inflation adjustment, so exposure is hard to quantify.

18. **§5(a) and §8:** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 doesn't take effect until 180 days later. It's unclear whether conduct in that window is penalized, and the penalty clause assumes a prohibition that isn't yet in force. The more natural reading is that no violation occurs before the effective date, but the text is inconsistent.

19. **§5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined. An operator acting on a good-faith reading of §3(b) or §3(c) would have a credible argument that it lacked willfulness, which narrows criminal exposure. The Act also has no provision allocating responsibility among corporate officers.

20. **§6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" is hortatory, with no consequence if no agreement is reached. "Equivalent" prohibitions is undefined, and the Act doesn't say whether a concluded agreement would change its operation. The provision is largely aspirational.

21. **§7(a):** "Serious harm" is undefined. The clause doesn't require NASEM to issue a report or set a deadline, and it doesn't say whether the joint resolution is presented to the President or what expedited procedures apply. As written, the prohibition has no defined exit, which is a substantive problem for us and a workability problem for the regime.

22. **§7(a) and §7(b):** These conflict. §7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until a joint resolution is enacted, while §7(b) says the Act ceases to have effect after 10 years. Read together, the prohibition could end at year 10 regardless of any NASEM finding. This reading favors us, but sponsors will likely fix it, and we shouldn't rely on it without a clear argument.

23. **§7(b) and §8:** The 10-year sunset runs from enactment, but the Act takes effect 180 days later, so the operative period is about 9.5 years. The Act has no savings clause for violations, penalties, or registry obligations accrued before the sunset.

24. **Whole Act (no severability clause):** If a court strikes one provision, such as the delegation in §2(1)(B) or the joint-resolution mechanism in §7(a), the fate of the rest is uncertain. Absence of severability also supports a broader facial challenge.

25. **Whole Act (relationship to existing law):** The Act doesn't say whether it amends, supersedes, or operates alongside the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.) or NOAA's existing DSHMRA regulations. This determines whether current authorizations survive and is probably the most consequential silence in the text.

26. **Whole Act (no rulemaking authority):** The Act doesn't authorize regulations to define key terms or implement the registry or the §3(c) exemption. The agency therefore has unclear authority to fill the gaps, which supports an argument that the Act is unworkable as drafted.

---

**Priorities for Thursday's markup (my assessment):**
- **#10 and #9:** The grandfathering clause is the most direct path to continued operations, and it's where we need the clearest textual argument.
- **#6 and #7:** The jurisdictional reach and the undefined "engage in" are the most concrete gaps.
- **#22 and #21:** The §7 conflict and the open-ended exit are strong talking points on workability.
- **#25:** Silence on DSHMRA could determine whether existing permits survive.
- **#18 and #19:** Penalty timing and the willfulness standard reduce exposure but are easy for sponsors to fix.

**Cautions:**
- Items that depend on contested readings (especially #22 and #7) are arguments, not certainties. Lead with defects that are clear on the face of the text.
- Pointing to vagueness is more persuasive when tied to specific operational consequences. Calling the bill "unworkable" in general terms will be easier for staff to dismiss.
- Several items (#15, #18, #22, #23) are the kind sponsors commonly fix at markup. Consider whether we want to raise them publicly or hold them for private negotiation.
- I haven't verified current DSHMRA regulations, Area contract structures, or the status of any pending permits. Legal should check those against our actual filings.
